name: Indefinite NP with a Modified Personal Name
pattern: NP[a/an + attributive AdjP + personal name form]

entry.name: Indefinite NP with a Modified Personal Name
entry.pattern: NP[a/an + attributive AdjP + personal name form]

1.definition: Presents a named person in a condition associated with a particular occasion.
1.details: In a visibly shaken Giuliani, the name identifies a person already introduced in the report. The adjective supplies his state within the NP, and the clause predicates what he did. One analysis takes the modifier to characterize the bearer directly. Another takes the NP to pick out a manifestation, understood as the bearer in one of several possible states.

examples.form: [A visibly shaken Giuliani] noted the tragic circumstances during a hospital press conference.
examples.note: The report has already named Rudolph Giuliani and described his emotional state.

grounds.locator: Paragraph before the quotation about Father’s Day

examples.note: The modified name is a preposition’s complement within the description of a photograph.
An evidential adverb can qualify the attribution made by the adjective.

grounds.locator: §7 [62], from the GB section of NOW, 23 February 2017

relatedConstructions.notes: The overt article takes determiner function in an NP with an adjective and a personal name form.
Poor Henry and a visibly shaken Giuliani both characterize an identifiable bearer. The former illustrates the restricted class of adjectives in bare embellishments.

The analyses overlap if a visibly shaken Giuliani selects one manifestation. In the Paris of my youth, a contextually delimited period is explicitly identified, whereas the CBS token provides an occasion-specific description in a report about a single event.

Both patterns can characterize a participant during an event. Compare They carried an unconscious Kim with They carried Kim unconscious. In the former, the adjective is internal to the object NP. In the latter, it is a secondary predicative outside that NP.

grounds.note: The selected COCA comparisons favour a/an with short-lived conditions. Berezowski analyses the contrast in terms of name-bearer manifestations and ordinary indefinite reference.
The authors discuss an angry Blair as nonrestrictive with respect to the person and contrastive with respect to that person’s possible states.
CGEL describes bare and the-marked adjectival embellishments and treats the selection of a manifestation separately.

projection.target: A temporary-state adjective can make a/an available with an already identified name bearer, in subject position and within a PP. The determiner choice varies with the adjective and the construal of its contribution.
projection.evidence: CBS supplies the previously identified bearer. Berezowski’s selected COCA comparisons give more a/an tokens than the or bare tokens for angry, smiling, beaming, relaxed and tired. His young and old comparisons are predominantly bare.

known_boundary_items: Poor Henry supplies an attribution in a bare NP. CGEL also gives the distraught Empress Alexandra with the and a temporary state.
Another Roosevelt describes a person by resemblance. A visibly shaken Giuliani keeps Giuliani as the bearer whose state is described.

curious.title: A shaken Giuliani, a smiling Johnson
curious.summary: Putting a or an and a describing word in front of a person's name can present that person in a particular state on a particular occasion.
curious.body: In A visibly shaken Giuliani noted the tragic circumstances, the name belongs to someone the report has already introduced. The describing word tells us his state at the time, and the rest of the sentence says what he did. Why a rather than the or nothing? One analysis says the description is directly about the person. Another says the phrase picks out one version of the person, as he was in one of several possible states. This dictionary treats the question as open. The pattern also turns up after prepositions, as in next to a smiling Hootie Johnson.

examples.text: [A visibly shaken Giuliani] noted the tragic circumstances during a hospital press conference.

curious.try: Think of a news photo caption. Could you write a smiling and a name there, such as a smiling Maria? What does adding the describing word tell you about that moment?

teacher.summary: For advanced classes, a or an with an adjective and a personal name, as in a visibly shaken Giuliani.
teacher.explain: The pattern is a noun phrase made of a or an, an attributive adjective phrase and a personal name form. The article is in determiner function. In the Giuliani example the name identifies a person already introduced in the report, and the adjective supplies his state on an occasion. This dictionary reports two analyses: the modifier characterizes the bearer directly, or the phrase picks out a manifestation, understood as the bearer in one of several possible states. It cites a corpus comparison in which a/an used with angry, smiling, beaming, relaxed and tired gives more tokens than the or bare forms, while young and old comparisons are predominantly bare. The analysis is provisional, so present the analysis as open.
teacher.terms: Sometimes discussed under the heading of proper names used with an indefinite article. This dictionary treats the whole phrase as a noun phrase in which a or an is the determiner.

examples.text: [A visibly shaken Giuliani] noted the tragic circumstances during a hospital press conference.

contrasts.note: The adjective is inside the object noun phrase.
The adjective is outside it, as a secondary predicative.

watch_for: A learner might read a smiling Hootie Johnson as introducing a second person with the same name.
A learner might treat unconscious in They carried Kim unconscious as part of the object noun phrase.
teacher.activity: Give students short news-style captions with a name and a temporary state. They rewrite each with the adjective after the name, as in the second contrast sentence, and say whether the adjective is inside or outside the noun phrase.
